synopsis: The introduction, Chapter 9 and glossary consistently frame collision-mitigation tuning as constrained multi-objective optimization: impose hard safety limits first, then optimize nuisance warnings, unnecessary braking and productivity while keeping the Pareto frontier visible [f136, f6671, f14395]. Hard limits cover stopping margin, miss probability, intervention latency and hazardous-scenario coverage; zero misses in critical scenarios is an example, not a universal numerical requirement [f6961, f6962, f14393]. Safety and productivity criteria must be set jointly: detection-only optimization can repeatedly stop production, while a “no false brakes” target pushes toward late or missed braking; pricing these competing outcomes is a documented safety-policy decision, with weight sensitivity analysis required if weighted costs are used [f12171, f7461, f6985, f14846]. Robust optimization should protect the worst stratum or a high percentile, and final settings should favor stable regions and be confirmed independently to limit over-fitting [f6988, f14400, f14403]. Evolutionary and Bayesian multi-objective methods suit expensive evaluations but weaken beyond about 20 parameters or with discontinuous responses; a 2021 on-road example reported up to fivefold speed-up, while no off-road evidence was identified for constraint-based tuning or desirability aggregation [f6674, f6839, f7316, f7311].

relations.note: Both make missed or late interventions constraints and optimize nuisance and productivity outcomes.
Both preserve the Pareto front instead of hiding trade-offs in weighted scores.
Pricing misses against nuisance braking is a documented safety-policy decision.
Both list thresholds, zones, confirmation filters, timing parameters and filter constants as decision variables.
Glossary restates the Chapter 9 tuning decision variables.
Both enumerate misses, nuisance rates, intervention timing and time stopped as outcomes.
Glossary restates Chapter 9 outcome measures, including productivity loss as time stopped.
Both specify stopping margin, miss probability, latency and hazardous-scenario coverage constraints.
Both optimize nuisance, comfort and productivity only after satisfying hard safety constraints.
Both require a visible Pareto frontier for engineering and safety authorities.
Both require sensitivity analysis when using weighted objectives.
Both find bounded-miss constraint formulations easier to defend than weighted costs.
Both protect weak strata through worst-case or high-percentile optimization rather than averages.
Both recommend joint safety and productivity acceptance criteria.
Defensible bounded-miss tuning requires a reliable miss estimate inside the tuning loop.
Repeated production stops explain why detection-only targets require joint acceptance criteria.
Subjective weights change the apparent optimum, motivating mandatory weight sensitivity analysis.
The recommended defensibility framing lacks identified off-road evidence, limiting its empirical backing.
